descriptions.text: $1.8 million walked out the door as Abracadabra’s deprecated Cauldron contracts let anyone flip a flag and borrow uncollateralized MIM. Three hacks, $21 million lost, and the simplest exploit yet proves some magic tricks are deadly obvious.

The Abracadabra Cauldron cook() function lets users batch actions. The exploit abuses the ACTION_REPAY (action 5) action combined with a no-op so that the solvency / borrow accounting was bypassed: the attacker was able to extract MIM (the protocol's BentoBox MIM share) from each Cauldron without leaving a corresponding solvent debt position. By looping over six Cauldrons and calling cook with a repay action crafted from each Cauldron's available BentoBox MIM balance (capped by borrowLimit), the attacker pulled out MIM shares, withdrew them from BentoBox to actual MIM, then routed MIM -> 3CRV (Curve) -> USDT -> WETH for ~1.7M USD. The core flaw is that the action sequence allowed state changes (MIM withdrawal) while the post-action insolvency/borrow check failed to catch the resulting under-collateralized state. Vulnerable code snippet: Attack Tx: https://etherscan.io/tx/0x842aae91c89a9e5043e64af34f53dc66daf0f033ad8afbf35ef0c93f99a9e5e6 Analysis: https://etherscan.io/address/0x46f54d434063e5f1a2b2cc6d9aaa657b1b9ff82c#code

On 2025-10-04, an attacker exploited Abracadabra's deprecated Ethereum CauldronV4 markets by borrowing MIM through cook() and then clearing the pending solvency check with a custom action. The linked exploit transaction drained 1,793,766.13 MIM and converted it into about 395.06 ETH. CauldronV4's batched cook() flow stored post-action safety in a mutable CookStatus struct. ACTION_BORROW set needsSolvencyCheck = true, but a later custom action path assigned the return value of _additionalCookAction(...) back to status, clearing that flag. The function then skipped the final _isSolvent(...) check and allowed MIM borrowing with recorded debt but no collateral.
